title: The Certainty Trap: Organisations Stop Learning
author: Jason L. Zimmerman
source: The Art of Asking Questions, Substack, July 18, 2026
summary: This article introduces the certainty trap—the organizational phenomenon by which pressure causes leadership teams to narrow their vision, centralize authority, and make high-velocity decisions based on partial information, thereby accelerating the very crisis they intended to solve. Using the example of a board with 48 hours to secure payroll, the article reframes what appeared to be a financial crisis as an epistemic one: a total breakdown in the organization's ability to know what was actually happening inside itself. The author maps pressure on a dial from one to ten, showing how each level progressively destroys curiosity, silos information, and reclassifies dissent as delay. Borrowing from wildland firefighting's LCES protocol—Lookouts, Communications, Escape Routes, Safety Zones—the article argues that organizational survival under pressure depends on maintaining distributed intelligence from the organizational edges, not centralizing command. Four diagnostic questions are offered as structural circuit breakers: shrinking the horizon, dropping legacy tools, consulting frontline lookouts, and red-teaming the current diagnosis.
points: The certainty trap describes how pressure causes leaders to act on partial truths with high confidence, believing they see the whole problem when they only see the most visible part—creating second and third-order consequences that amplify the original disaster.

Barry Staw's research shows organizations under threat naturally restrict information flow, centralize authority, and rely on familiar routines—exactly the opposite of what complex, novel crises require.

Wildland firefighting's LCES protocol demonstrates that speed and distributed intelligence are not opposites: the junior lookout on a distant ridge can override the command post's strategic plan in real time.

Four diagnostic questions act as structural circuit breakers under duress: shrink the horizon to 24-hour problems, drop legacy tools, consult the frontline lookout, and red-team the current diagnosis by assuming it is wrong.
The fundamental test of leadership under pressure is not whether an executive can produce a confident answer—most can—but whether they can preserve the organization's intelligence while doing it.
quotes: The crisis wasn’t driven by inferior service or bad frontline delivery. This was a pure liquidity stranglehold.

When you reach that level of duress, pressure does something dangerous to human cognition: it destroys the capacity to see clearly. Speed pulls against accuracy, while anxiety narrows what leaders can see.

Staw's work demonstrates that organisations under threat naturally restrict information, rely on familiar routines and centralise control. Meanwhile, Weick explains that, under acute stress, our collective capacity to make sense of an unfolding reality completely collapses.

In a disciplined system, the data provided by the lookout can instantly override the strategic plan of the command post. Speed is maintained, but it is explicitly bound to real-time, distributed data from the edges.

The fundamental test of leadership under duress is not whether an executive can produce a confident answer. Most can. The harder, more significant question is whether they can preserve the organisation’s intelligence while doing it.

The crisis in that room was treated as a financial one. In reality, it was an epistemic crisis: a total breakdown in the organisation’s ability to know what was actually happening inside its own walls.
